title: Blame only the rules people can change

blocks.text: A school's timetabling model has two kinds of rules. **Hard** rules are physics and law: a room holds one class at a time, a teacher works at most six periods. **Soft** rules are requests someone made and could withdraw: "7A only in the mornings", "the lab is closed on Tuesday". When the timetable has no solution, the deputy head wants a conflict made of soft rules only, the ones a person can change, read together with every hard rule.

You get an oracle, `infeasible(rules) -> bool`, which says whether the timetable has no solution when exactly the rules in the set `rules` are switched on. Write `conflict_among(soft, hard, infeasible)`:

items: if all the rules together are feasible, return `None`;
if the hard rules alone are already infeasible, return `[]` (no soft rule is to blame);
otherwise run a deletion filter over the soft rules, in the order given, with every hard rule switched on in every question, and return the soft rules that are left, in the order given.

blocks.text: What is left must be irreducible among the soft rules: with the hard rules on, the kept soft rules are infeasible, and dropping any one of them makes them feasible. About twelve lines.

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Callable


def conflict_among(soft: list[str], hard: list[str], infeasible: Callable[[set[str]], bool]) -> list[str] | None:
    """The soft rules of one irreducible conflict, with every hard rule always on.

    None if all the rules together are feasible; [] if the hard rules alone are infeasible.
    """
    always, kept = set(hard), list(soft)
    if not infeasible(always | set(kept)):
        return None
    if infeasible(always):
        return []
    for rule in soft:
        if infeasible(always | (set(kept) - {rule})):      # still infeasible without it: it goes
            del kept[kept.index(rule)]
    return kept


if __name__ == "__main__":
    clash = [{"room_cap_B12", "class_7A_in_B12"}]
    print(conflict_among(["class_7A_in_B12", "teacher_off_fri"], ["room_cap_B12"],
                         lambda on: any(c <= on for c in clash)))

import logging

# Turn the logger up, so the `log.debug` lines of your code show under the printed lines.
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG, format="%(levelname)s %(message)s")

from timetable import conflict_among

soft = ["9C_afternoons", "9C_gym_wed", "gym_shut_wed", "10D_gym_wed"]
hard = ["one_class_per_room", "teacher_max_5"]


def oracle(*clashes):
    sets = [set(c) for c in clashes]
    return lambda on: any(c <= set(on) for c in sets)


print("conflict, gym shut on Wednesday:", conflict_among(soft, hard, oracle(["9C_gym_wed", "gym_shut_wed"])))
print("conflict, two classes in the gym:",
      conflict_among(soft, hard, oracle(["9C_gym_wed", "10D_gym_wed", "one_class_per_room"])))
print("conflict, nothing clashes:", conflict_among(soft, hard, oracle(["no_such_rule"])))

cases.says: the soft rules of a conflict come back in their given order, and a feasible timetable gives None
a conflict can need a hard rule, so the hard rules are in every question
with two separate conflicts the filter must end with one of them

origin.section: The Additive Filter Builds a Conflict From Nothing

concepts: a deletion filter over the rules people can change, with the fixed rules in every question
